studies.title: A Watch Over Every Soul
studies.meaning: The oath names something and then refuses to identify it. A question intervenes, and only in the third line does the answer arrive, two words wide: the piercing star. Classical commentators take the sworn object as a star visible at night, the name carrying the sense of something that arrives after dark. What the oath supports is a single claim about every human being without exception: a keeper is set over the soul. Readers differ over whether that keeper is a recording angel or God's own preservation, and the sources hold both.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and early. The short surahs of this period open with oaths sworn on things the audience could see, then land a claim they had not conceded. Mecca at the time had no organised opposition yet, only mockery, and the recitations were heard in the open air near the sanctuary. The classical sources report no particular occasion for these lines and read them as part of the first argument for accountability.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to strike. A traveller arriving after dark announced himself by knocking, so the word names a visitor who comes at night, and the sky is sworn by alongside it.
The root covers boring through and burning bright. Commentators read both: a star whose light pierces the darkness, or one that pierces the sky itself. The intensity is in the word, not added.

An active participle from the root of preserving, the same root behind memorising. It names one who holds something intact, which is why the readings divide between a guard who protects and a recorder who retains.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night travel was normal. Caravans moved after sunset to spare the animals, steered by stars whose risings were known by name, and a house woken at that hour by a knock knew the news would be urgent. Guarding was equally familiar: flocks needed a watch, and a merchant leaving on a season's journey left someone behind who was answerable for the household. The oath borrows both pictures at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The formula that asks what will let you know something occurs a dozen times in the Quran, and it is not always answered at once. Here the answer comes in the very next line, two words long. In surah 82 the same question about the Day of Judgement is asked twice over, one line after the other, before anything is said.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The claim is framed as a double negative: there is no soul but that a keeper is over it. Stating it that way closes the exception before anyone can look for one. It also relocates the argument. The oath is cosmic, sworn on the sky and a star, and the conclusion is interior and personal. Nothing about a person's life is unattended, and that is presented as a fact of creation rather than a threat.

crossReferences.why: Names the keepers directly as noble recorders who know whatever a person does.
Describes successive guardians before and behind a person, keeping him by God's command.
Places a watcher beside every word spoken, ready at the moment it is said.

studies.applyIt: Tonight, when the house is quiet, take the one thing you did today that nobody saw and hold it in mind for a minute. Not to judge it. Just to notice that it happened, that it was real, and that it went somewhere rather than nowhere. Most of a life is made of those unwitnessed minutes.

studies.title: The Day Secrets Are Tested
studies.meaning: An argument runs from origin to return in three short steps. Look at what you were made from; it was a liquid, described by a participle of spurting; therefore the one who did that can do it again. The classical commentators treat the second creation as the easier of the two, since nothing was there the first time. Then the day is named by what happens to interiors rather than to bodies, and the passage closes by stripping away both of the things a person under threat would reach for: force of his own, and someone to stand with him.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Resurrection was the point the audience refused, and the surahs of this period return to it from different directions rather than repeating a proof. Here the approach is biological and domestic: the argument starts from a fact about themselves that nobody disputed. The commentators record no specific occasion, placing the passage within the long Meccan argument about whether scattered bones can be gathered.

keyTerms.note: An active participle of forceful, intermittent flow, used of water driven out under pressure. The English word liquid is neutral; the Arabic adds motion, so the origin is described as an event rather than a substance.
The verb belongs to the root of trial and assaying, not to the root of announcing. Secrets are not merely published on that day; they are put to the test, the way a metal is.
A plural of what is hidden, from the root behind confiding in someone. It reaches past hidden deeds to intentions, so what is examined includes things the person never acted on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in Mecca was a public ledger. A man's lineage was recited, his generosity was reported at gatherings, and poets were paid to fix a version of him in verse that would outlive him. There was almost no privacy of walls, but there was enormous privacy of motive: nobody could check why a host had been lavish. A day that assays motives cut across the only asset many of them had.
studies.didYouKnow: The description of where that liquid issues from, between the backbone and the ribs, is one of the passages where the classical commentators openly disagree. Some read the two parts as belonging to the man, some divide them between man and woman, and some take the phrase as locating the process in the body generally. Al-Tabari lists the views without choosing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Power over the future is argued from the past rather than asserted. The passage does not ask for trust in a claim about resurrection; it asks for a look backwards at something already done. Its second move is moral rather than physical. If judgement examines what was concealed, then the self that matters is not the public one, and the social machinery for managing reputation has nothing to work on.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same argument at greater length, from a drop of fluid to the power to revive the dead.
Answers the question about decayed bones by pointing back at the first creation.
Pairs the scattering of graves with the bringing out of what is inside the chests.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you did this week that other people praised, and ask yourself quietly what you actually wanted from it. Do not perform an answer. Most motives are mixed, and seeing the mixture is the whole exercise. You are practising, in a small way, the kind of looking the passage says will happen anyway.

studies.title: A Word That Decides
studies.meaning: Two more oaths open a second half, and both are about things that open and close. The sky is sworn by as possessing return, which most classical readers take as rain, since the sky gives back the water it drew up; a minority read it as the circling of what moves across it. The earth is sworn by as possessing splitting, the crust broken by a shoot. What the pair supports is a claim about the recitation itself. It separates, and it is not entertainment.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The recitation was being filed by its first hearers under categories they already had: poetry, soothsaying, the rhymed speech of a diviner, something to be enjoyed at a gathering and argued over afterwards. These lines refuse all of that in two words. The classical sources describe the Meccan leadership discussing among themselves what to call it, precisely because no existing label fitted.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun of returning something. Applied to the sky it makes rain a restitution rather than a gift, water handed back to the ground that lost it, which is why most commentators read it that way.
The root names a crack in something solid, and the same word covers a rift in a group of people. Here it is the crust of dry ground broken from underneath by what is growing.
A noun from the root of cutting apart, used of a judge's ruling that ends a dispute. Calling the speech itself a separation makes it an act rather than a message about one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a rainless year a family ate its capital: the breeding stock went first, then the date palms were mortgaged. When rain finally came, the wadi floor split within days and the greening was visible from the ridge. Everyone in the audience had waited on that cycle and could date their own lives by it. Poetry, meanwhile, was the entertainment of the season, judged at fairs and prized for the pleasure it gave.
studies.didYouKnow: This seventeen-ayah surah carries two separate clusters of oaths, one at its opening and one here at the start of its second half, each followed by the claim it supports. That doubled structure is unusual; most short surahs swear once and then argue. The second cluster is the shorter of the two and the claim it introduces is the shortest in the surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described here as having a function rather than a content. It divides, the way a verdict divides a case, which means a hearer cannot stay where he was standing. The denial that follows is equally pointed: the opposite of a decisive word is not a false one but an amusing one. Speech that entertains leaves everything as it was, and that is the category being refused.

crossReferences.why: Rejects the same misfilings by name, denying that the recitation is the speech of a poet or a diviner.
Uses the split earth and returning rain together as the standing image of raising the dead.
Names the revelation by the word for what separates truth from falsehood, the same idea in a title.

studies.applyIt: Choose a passage you have heard so often that it has become background noise, and read it once as though a decision followed from it. Ask what it settles, not what it says. If nothing in your week would look different, sit with that for a moment rather than resolving it. Notice what it asks of you today.

studies.title: Give Them A Little Time
studies.meaning: The reply reuses the opponents' own word. They are scheming a scheme, and the answer is that God schemes too. Classical commentators are careful here: the matching is a feature of Arabic, which answers an act with its own name, and what is meant of God is the just undoing of a plot, not deceit. Then the instruction. Not retaliation, not a curse, but a command to grant delay, given twice in two different verb forms and then cut down by a final word meaning only a little.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the years when opposition had moved past argument into organised pressure: boycott, the harrying of the vulnerable among the believers, and discussions among the leadership about what to do with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The classical sources attach no single occasion to these two lines and read them as the standing instruction of that period, when the community had no means of answering and was told not to look for one.

keyTerms.note: The word covers contrivance of any kind, from a trick to a strategy, and takes its moral colour from its object. Repeating it for both sides is an Arabic figure that answers an act with its own name.
An intensive verb of giving time, from a root about acting slowly. It asks for deliberate delay rather than passive waiting, and it is addressed to the one with the grievance.
A diminutive of a word for gentleness and slowness, and it occurs nowhere else in the Quran. It shrinks the respite just granted, so the last sound of the surah is the smallness of the delay.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Tribal Arabia ran on the speed of the answer. An injury unanswered was read as an injury the group could not answer, and once that reading settled, more injuries followed. Feuds were remembered in verse for generations and revived by a single line recited at the right gathering. To be told to wait, without a date, in a society where delay meant weakness, was to be told to accept a public cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The command to give respite is issued twice in a single line, first with one verb pattern and then with another from the same root, before the qualifier arrives. Arabic uses that kind of doubling for emphasis, and here the emphasis falls on restraint rather than on threat, which is unusual for the closing line of a surah about plotting.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held apart that human beings normally fuse: the certainty that a wrong will be answered, and the right to answer it yourself. The first is affirmed in the strongest terms; the second is quietly removed. What remains for the wronged party is time, and time is presented as something God is spending deliberately. The passage also refuses to say how long, which is where its difficulty sits.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction in almost the same words, pairing patience with leaving the deniers a short while.
Explains a granted delay from the other side, as time that lets a course of action complete itself.
Warns against reading a postponement as inattention, since the delay runs to a fixed day.

studies.applyIt: Think of the message you have drafted in your head to someone who wronged you, the one you keep rehearsing. Do not send it today. Do not decide never to send it either. Just move it to tomorrow, once, and watch what the extra day does to the wording. That is the whole practice this line asks for.
